newsitem.title: USA: Revamped Dow ends higher, shakes off rate concerns.
newsitem.headline: Revamped Dow ends higher, shakes off rate concerns.

text.p: The revamped Dow industrials ended higher on Monday, fending off concerns over rising interest rates and market views that stocks have become too expensive.
On the first day of trading with four new components, the Dow 30 rose 20 points, or 0.3 percent, to 6955. The blue-chip index posted a late rally after falling as much as 80 points.
But other measures reflected broad weakness in U.S. stocks, particularily in high-technology shares. Losing issues outnumbered gainers by a two-to-one ratio on the NYSE.

The Nasdaq composite, reflecting losses in tech stocks, finished down more than 13 points, or 1.1 percent, to 1279. Among leading high-tech names, Intel Corp shed 1-1/2 to 136-3/8 after hitting a low of 131-3/4.

The weakness in the broader market was a sign investors are eager to take profit in stocks with high price/earnings multiples ahead of the March 25 meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy making committee, analysts said.
High tech stocks "have lost momentum and nobody's willing to step up here," said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manager at Unity Management. "All eyes are on next week's Fed meeting."
Fed officials are expected to debate whether to raise short-term interest rates at the meeting.

In an indication of stocks' sensitivity to interest rates, the Dow rallied in late trading after the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rebounded after the yield briefly hit the psychologically important 7.0 percent level. The long bond was off 6/32 in late trading, yielding 6.96 percent.

One market player citing pricey stock levels was billionaire financier Warren Buffett, who commented in an annual letter to stockholders of his Berkshire Hathaway Inc that he views most stocks as overvalued.
"Buffett is a sage a lot of people take to heart," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray and Co.

Stocks tend to rise, however, heading into a triple expiration of equity and index options and index futures, which is due on Friday, said Harry Laubscher, market analyst at Tucker Anthony. "I would anticipate some firmness but nothing getting out of hand because people are still concerned about what happens next week," he said.
Monday's trading marked the debut as Dow components of Hewlett-Packard Co, Travelers Group Inc, Johnson and Johnson and Wal-Mart Stores Inc.

The stocks replaced four stocks in the blue chip index. Hewlett-Packard finished up 1/4 to 55-5/8, Travelers eased 1-3/8 to 51-7/8, Johnson and Johnson ended unchanged at 57-7/8 and Wal-Mart rose 1/4 to 28-7/8.
Wall Street was hit by a wave of merger-related news Monday.

Tyco International Ltd said it was acquiring ADT Ltd in a stock deal valued at $5.4 billion. Tyco, a maker of fire and safety systems, fell two to 58-1/4. ADT, a provider of electronic security services, gained 3-7/8 to 25-5/8.

H.F. Ahmanson & Co raised its hostile bid for Great Western Financial Corp, in an offer that it said topped a rival "white knight" bid by Washington Mutual Savings Bank. Washington Mutual said it was not planning to raise its bid, saying it was confident its deal would prevail.
Ahmanson fell 1/2 to 39-3/4. Great Western slipped 1/4 to 45-1/4, while Washington Mutual ended up 3/4 to 51-1/8.
Valero Energy Corp agreed to buy Basis Petroleum Inc from Salomon Inc in a deal valued at $485 million.

Salomon said it would restate its fourth quarter results due to the sale and that it expects an after-tax loss of $290 million from the deal. But analysts said the sale would allow Salomon to focus on its core businesses, including securities trading and investment banking. Salomon ended down 1-1/2 to 52-5/8 and Valero rose 1-1/8 to 33-7/8.
Credit card company Advanta Corp sank 8-1/2 to 31-7/8 after it surprised Wall Street with news that it expects to post a loss of $0.44 a share in 1997's first quarter.
The S&P 500 index rose 2.54 points to 795.71.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
